abstract: METR announces they are redesigning their developer productivity experiment due to severe selection effects that made their data unreliable. Their original 2025 study found a 19% slowdown, but the follow-up study reveals this was likely an artifact of experimental design. New data from 57 developers across 800+ tasks shows estimated speedups, not slowdowns, though wide confidence intervals span zero. The authors explicitly state their current data gives an 'unreliable signal' of AI's productivity impact.
keyFindings: METR retracts the reliability of their original 19% slowdown finding, stating data gives 'unreliable signal of the current productivity effect of AI tools'
Original developers from early 2025 study now show estimated -18% speedup (CI: -38% to +9%), reversing the earlier slowdown finding
Newly-recruited developers show estimated -4% speedup (CI: -15% to +9%)
30-50% of developers reported avoiding submitting tasks they expected AI to accelerate, creating severe downward selection bias
Recruitment and retention became harder as developers increasingly refused to work without AI tools
Authors conclude their estimate is 'likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact of AI tools on these developers'
METR is exploring alternative study designs: intensive short experiments, observational data, questionnaires, fixed-task experiments, developer-level randomization
methodology: Follow-up study from August 2025 with 57 developers (10 from original study, 47 newly recruited) across 143 open-source repositories and 800+ tasks. Participants paid $50/hour (down from $150/hour in original). Tasks randomized into AI-allowed or AI-disallowed conditions. Compared against original Feb-June 2025 study with 16 developers and 246 tasks.
qualifiers: Authors explicitly acknowledge the data is unreliable due to multiple selection effects: developer self-selection out of the study, task-level selection bias (developers avoid submitting high-uplift tasks), lower pay rate ($50 vs $150/hr), changes in task types with AI, variable code quality between conditions, and difficulty measuring time with concurrent AI agents. The true speedup could be much higher than measured.
